rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the six-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing late compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

The first method already reaches the maximum CRF, with ample resolution margin. Shorten the gradient while holding the window and temperature fixed to test whether full resolution can be retained in a faster run.
The 6-minute gradient retains full resolution and maximum CRF. Test a 4-minute gradient to shorten the run further while checking whether the critical early pair remains above R = 1.5.

The 4-minute gradient still achieves maximum CRF, but the early pair is close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test for a shorter fully resolved run and measure temperature-dependent selectivity.

Heating reduced the critical early-pair resolution, so test the lowest temperature to favor its separation while shortening to the minimum gradient duration. This probes whether improved selectivity can offset gradient compression; injection 3 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.
Narrow the gradient window to reduce its slope and improve the early pair’s R = 1.23 while retaining the 2-minute gradient. Keep phi1 at 0.95 to promote rapid elution of the last compound.
Injection 6 achieves maximum CRF at the minimum gradient duration. Raise phi0 one step to test a slightly faster elution window while monitoring the early pair for loss of retention or resolution.

Raise temperature by one step to shorten the run while using the early pair’s resolution margin of 1.77. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect near this fast, maximum-CRF method.

Test one higher starting organic fraction to shorten the run and determine whether narrowing the gradient still improves the critical pair. The first peak is already near the unretained region, so this probes the upper useful limit of phi0; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return phi0 to 0.30 to restore early-peak retention, then test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method. This locates the temperature limit for maintaining R >= 1.5 in the critical early pair.

Reduce gradient steepness to recover the early pair’s resolution at 35 C without increasing gradient duration. Monitor the last peak for extra hold-time retention; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Shift the window lower while preserving injection 11’s slope to retain the early pair longer and test whether its resolution recovers above 1.5. The strong final solvent should still elute the last compound well within the 10-minute scoring limit.

Refine around injection 8, the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, by lowering phi1 one step to seek more early-pair resolution margin. This should retain maximum CRF with only a small increase in last-peak retention.

Lower phi0 one step from injection 13 to move the first peak away from the unretained region while retaining a fast gradient. Test whether this alternative preserves full resolution and maximum CRF with better early-peak retention.

Maximum CRF is already achieved; test a short-run alternative with more resolution margin by combining lower temperature and a shallower gradient. Starting at phi0 = 0.25 also keeps the early peaks farther from the unretained region than the fastest confirmed method, injection 8.

Raise phi1 one step from injection 15 to accelerate the last peak while retaining some of its early-pair resolution margin. This tests a faster alternative with better initial retention than injection 8, which remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Test whether the stronger endpoint can shorten injection 14 while preserving its marginal early-pair resolution. This completes the local comparison around injection 8, the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method, with a lower starting organic fraction.

Lower temperature from injection 13 to improve the critical early pair’s resolution while maintaining a short run. This tests a higher-margin maximum-CRF alternative; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a lower starting organic fraction than injection 6 to improve early-peak retention while keeping the strongest endpoint and minimum gradient duration. The early pair may approach the resolution threshold, but this could provide another fully resolved method with the last peak near 2.7 minutes.

Lower phi1 one step from injection 19 to improve its borderline early-pair resolution while preserving good initial retention. This tests a higher-margin maximum-CRF alternative with only a modest expected increase in last-peak time.

Lower phi1 one step from injection 18 to test additional early-pair resolution margin while keeping the minimum gradient duration. Maximum CRF is already established; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 21 to shorten last-peak retention while testing whether its early-pair resolution margin remains sufficient. This also brackets the temperature limit at this window, since 35 C failed in injection 11.

Lower phi0 one step from injection 22 to retain the early peaks farther from the solvent front while testing whether full resolution is preserved. This refines the short-run maximum-CRF region without repeating a method; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Reduce phi1 one step from injection 20 to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin while retaining the early peaks away from the solvent front. This tests another short maximum-CRF alternative; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 24 to shorten retention while testing whether its resolution margin preserves maximum CRF. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
